title: Tree of a Single Value
statement: You get the root of a non-empty binary tree. Return true if every node in the tree holds the same value, and false otherwise.

examples.why: The 5 is a grandchild of the root. Checking only the root's children would miss it.
A single node trivially agrees with itself.

hints: Which value must every node match?
Every node must equal the root's value. Visit them all.
Any traversal works: DFS with a stack or recursion, or BFS with a queue. Return false the moment a node differs from the root.

explain.intuition:
If all values are equal, they all equal the root's value. So read root.val once and visit every node, comparing against it. Stop early on the first mismatch.

A recursive version is just as natural: a subtree is single-valued if its root matches the target and both of its subtrees are single-valued. The important part is to go all the way down, not only one level: the mismatch can hide in any leaf.
steps: Push the root onto a stack.
Pop a node; if its value is not target, return false. Otherwise push its non-null children.
When the stack is empty, return true.
pitfalls: Only comparing the root with its two children.
Comparing each node with its parent but skipping one of the two subtrees in the recursion.
Short-circuiting the recursion with && is fine, but returning only the left subtree's result is not.

complexity.space: O(h) for DFS, O(width) for BFS

solutions.title: Recursive check
solutions.idea: A subtree is single-valued if its root equals the target and both children's subtrees are too.

solutions.title: Iterative walk with a stack
solutions.idea: Visit every node with an explicit stack and stop at the first value that differs from the root.

followups: Count how many subtrees are single-valued. What must each recursive call return?
Return the largest single-valued subtree's size.
